analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security payroll taxes, especially on high earners, and boosts benefits for low earners, students, and long-time beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for nearly two years without a hearing or vote, and was sent to a subcommittee only in the session's final week.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the Social Security payroll tax gradually from 6.2% to 6.5% for both workers and employers, and would phase out the cap on wages subject to that tax, so people earning above roughly $160,000 would pay Social Security tax on more of their income. The added money would fund a higher minimum benefit for people who worked many years at low wages, a 5% boost for people who have been on Social Security for 16 years or more, and an extension of child benefits to age 26 for full-time students. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Lifetime low earners would get a new minimum benefit pegged to the poverty line, scaled up with years worked (including years caring for young children). Beneficiaries who have received benefits for 16 years or more would get a boost of up to 5% of the average benefit. Children of retired, disabled, or deceased workers could keep receiving benefits through age 26 while in full-time college. The phase-out of the taxable earnings cap would also improve the program's long-term finances.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a new special minimum benefit for lifetime low earners, set as a percentage of the poverty guideline and rising with years worked, counting up to five years of childcare, so a 30-year worker could not be paid less than the poverty line [S3].

Increases monthly benefits by 5% of a benchmark amount for beneficiaries who have been eligible for 16 years, reaching the full increase after 20 years, recognizing that early benefits are eroded by years of lower cost-of-living growth [S3].
Lets children of retired, disabled, or deceased workers receive benefits through age 26 while full-time post-secondary students, instead of cutting off at 19 [S2][S3].

Raises the payroll tax rate to 6.5% (13% for the self-employed) by 2029 and applies it to earnings above the current cap, phasing in over a decade, with benefits calculated to reflect the newly taxed higher earnings [S2][S3].
Bars any benefit increase from being counted as income against eligibility for Medicaid, SNAP, or other means-tested programs, so the raises would not be clawed back [S3].

analysis.who_pays: All workers and their employers would pay a gradually higher payroll tax, from 6.2% to 6.5% on each side by 2029. Workers earning above the taxable maximum (about $160,200 in 2023) would pay Social Security tax on an increasing share of earnings above the cap, reaching all of it by 2034. Self-employed people would pay both sides.

drawbacks.text: The payroll tax increase applies to every worker's wages, not just high earners, so a household earning $50,000 would pay about $150 more per year by 2029, and employers' matching share may partly come out of wages [S3].

For earnings above the cap, the bill applies only a 3% benefit formula (compared with 90% and 32% below it), so high earners would pay far more in tax than they would get back, weakening the tax-to-benefit link that historically underpins Social Security's political support [S3].

Critics of lifting the earnings cap argue it changes Social Security toward a more redistributive program and could face employer objections to the higher matching tax, though no such opposition is recorded in the bill's history [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a modest, broadly shared tax increase (0.3 percentage points per side, phased over six years) for substantially higher benefits aimed at the poorest beneficiaries, plus student benefits through age 26 and a stronger revenue base from high earners. The main cost falls on ordinary workers in the form of a slightly larger paycheck deduction and on employers. The 3% benefit rate on earnings above the cap is a deliberate design choice that makes the bill more redistributive; an honest supporter would acknowledge it asks high earners to pay much more than they will ever receive.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, sat there for almost two years with no hearing or markup, and on December 17, 2024 — with days left in the Congress — was referred to its Social Security Subcommittee, where it died.

narrative.text: Rep. Gwen Moore introduced the bill on January 31, 2023, with Rep. Jan Schakowsky as an original cosponsor [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
The bill gained only two Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support [S4].
After 22 months with no committee action, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security on December 17, 2024, less than three weeks before the Congress ended [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners whose wages above the roughly $160,000 cap would have become taxable, and employers who would have faced the higher matching payroll tax, are better off because the bill never advanced. Workers who would have paid the higher rate are also spared the cost, but the low earners, long-time beneficiaries, and students the bill would have helped gain nothing.

industries.industry: High earners above the payroll tax cap
industries.note: The bill would phase out the taxable earnings cap, applying Social Security tax to wages above roughly $160,200, while giving above-cap earnings only a 3% benefit rate. Their tax burden under the bill funds benefits for others.

Employers' matching Social Security tax would rise from 6.2% to 6.5% by 2029 on all covered wages, and beyond the cap as it phases out. Standard economic analysis treats part of employer payroll taxes as ultimately borne by workers through lower wages.

industries.industry: Self-employed workers and small business owners
industries.note: They pay both the employee and employer shares, which would rise from 12.4% to 13.0%, though the phase-out of the cap mostly raises their taxes only above the earnings threshold.
